name: Travoprost

lead: Travoprost is a synthetic prostaglandin F2-alpha analog used as an eye drop to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. It is sold as Travatan and, as a surgical implant, as iDose TR.

The appearance angle is a side effect: prostaglandin analogs in this class can thicken and darken eyelashes. Travoprost's clinical research is about eye pressure; no trial has studied it for lashes, brows or scalp hair.

paras: In medical use, one drop is placed in the affected eye once a day, in the evening. An implant that releases travoprost for up to three years also exists. Any lash change appears as a side effect of that eye treatment rather than a purpose-built cosmetic product.

Common side effects are red eyes, blurred vision, eye pain, dry eyes and eye color change. It can permanently darken the iris to brown and permanently darken or thicken eyelashes. Use in pregnancy or breastfeeding is generally not recommended, and it is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia.

chain: Prostaglandin F2-alpha analog applied as an eye drop
Eyelash follicles respond as a side effect
angle.text: Eyelash thickening and darkening are listed side effects of travoprost eye drops. This is why prostaglandin eye drops come up in lash discussions, although the drug is prescribed for glaucoma.

lead: Travoprost is a synthetic analog of prostaglandin F2-alpha, an ester prodrug that becomes an active acid in the eye. It increases the outflow of aqueous fluid and lowers eye pressure, and is used for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension [1][2]. It was approved in the US and EU in 2001 and is sold as Travatan [1].

Its link to appearance is a documented side effect: thickening and permanent darkening of the eyelashes, and a possible permanent darkening of the iris to brown [1]. The same drug class gave rise to a cosmetic eyelash treatment: ophthalmologists noticed that people using prostaglandin-analog eye drops grew longer, fuller, darker lashes, and a related compound, bimatoprost, was later studied and approved for eyelash hypotrichosis [3][4][5]. Travoprost belongs to the same family, which is why it comes up when people discuss lash, brow and periocular hair changes. Clinical trials of travoprost describe eyelash changes and ocular hyperaemia as mostly mild adverse events [2].

The research on travoprost itself concerns eye pressure. Trials have compared it with timolol, latanoprost, bimatoprost and tafluprost [2][6][7][8], and a travoprost intracameral implant has been tested in phase 3 trials [8]. The lash-growth literature comes mainly from bimatoprost trials and from case reports on prostaglandin analogs generally; no published randomized trial has examined travoprost for cosmetic lash or hair growth. The class also carries documented periocular effects beyond lashes, including skin darkening and changes in the fat around the eye, which clinicians call prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy [9][10].
infobox: Isopropyl ester, converted to free acid in the eye [1]
Eyelash thickening and darkening; iris darkening [1]

paras: Travoprost is used to lower raised intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. It can be given with timolol when pressure is not adequately controlled [1][2]. The iDose TR intracameral implant is placed surgically and releases travoprost continuously for up to about three years [11].

Eyelash thickening and darkening and darker iris color are documented side effects [1]. Wikipedia's article on the related drug latanoprost notes that it lengthens and thickens eyelashes and that, like bimatoprost, prostaglandin analogs are used in the cosmetic industry as eyelash enhancers [12]. Travoprost itself is not marketed for cosmetic use.

subs.h: Related cosmetic use of the drug class
paras: Bimatoprost, a prostamide analog of the same family, is the compound that was developed into an approved prescription lash treatment. A review in Indian Dermatology Online Journal notes that increased eyelid pigmentation and hypertrichosis seen in glaucoma patients opened applications in dermatology, including conditions affecting the eyelashes and eyebrows [5]. Wikipedia reports that US approval of the cosmetic lash formulation is for hypotrichosis and that eyebrow use has been described in case reports [3].

Travoprost is hydrolysed in the eye to its free acid, which acts on FP prostanoid receptors to increase fluid outflow and lower pressure [1]. Wikipedia lists its effect onset at about two hours, with a duration of at least a day and very low systemic exposure [1].

The dermatology literature on prostaglandin analogs describes lash growth in terms of the drugs promoting the growth phase of the lash cycle; Wikipedia notes that the way bimatoprost acts on the eye is itself not fully understood [3]. In the 12-month bimatoprost trial, lash effects were maintained for about two months and markedly diminished four to six months after stopping [13].

After corneal absorption the active acid peaks in the eye within one to two hours, with a half-life in aqueous fluid of about 1.5 hours and a terminal half-life of about 45 minutes; systemic levels stay very low and the drug is excreted mainly by the kidneys [1].

Common side effects are red eyes, blurred vision, eye pain, dry eyes and eye color change. Other effects include eyelid redness and burning, and cataracts are listed. Use in pregnancy or breastfeeding is generally not recommended [1].

Permanent darkening of eyelashes and of the iris is listed for travoprost [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, reports eyelash lengthening, darkening and thickening in about half to three-quarters of treated patients in comparative studies and iris darkening mainly in people with lighter or mixed iris colors [14]. Wikipedia's articles on travoprost, bimatoprost and latanoprost all describe research in which wiping excess fluid from the eyelid after application was associated with shorter eyelashes and less eyelid hyperpigmentation [1][3][12].

Prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy is the name given to a cluster of changes around the eye in people who use these drops long-term, including deepening of the upper eyelid fold, drooping of the eyelid, lower-lid fat flattening and sunken-looking orbits. A case series of latanoprost users reported these changes after a mean of six years and stated that latanoprost carries a lower risk and longer onset than bimatoprost and travoprost; it also noted that using the drops in only one eye can produce visible asymmetry [9]. A 2024 review by Asian glaucoma specialists describes the lack of a consensus grading system for this syndrome and proposes adding patient-reported symptoms and measurements such as exophthalmometry to staging [10]. A 2024 clinical comparison of lash overgrowth (megalotrichosis) in six patients treated with prostaglandins and five treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors reported that poliosis, whitening of lashes, characterised the prostaglandin group and that onset was later, at a median of 440 days versus 176 days [15].

A Drugs & Aging review found travoprost 0.004% once daily significantly more effective than placebo or twice-daily timolol and at least as effective as latanoprost, with ocular hyperaemia and eyelash changes the most common mostly mild adverse events [2]. A network meta-analysis compared first-line glaucoma eye drops across 114 randomized trials with 20,275 participants [7]. A randomized trial in latanoprost non-responders compared latanoprost, travoprost and bimatoprost [6].

A phase 3 randomized trial of a travoprost intraocular implant (two release-rate models, 200 and 197 eyes) found mean pressure reductions of about 6.6 to 8.5 mmHg versus 6.5 to 7.7 mmHg with twice-daily timolol (193 eyes), meeting its non-inferiority endpoint [8]. A 2025 review lists the travoprost implant among newly approved glaucoma treatments, with an effect lasting nearly three years [11]. None of these trials measured lashes or hair as an outcome.

Cosmetic lash trials were done with bimatoprost, not travoprost. In a 5-month randomized, vehicle-controlled trial of 278 adults, 78.1 percent of bimatoprost 0.03% users versus 18.4 percent of vehicle users had at least a one-grade improvement in global eyelash assessment at week 16, with digital measurements of length, thickness and darkness as secondary outcomes [4]. A patient-reported outcomes analysis of the same trial found significantly greater satisfaction with length, fullness, confidence and attractiveness in the bimatoprost group [16]. A 12-month trial including people with chemotherapy-induced hypotrichosis reported responder rates of 40.2 percent versus 6.8 percent for vehicle in idiopathic hypotrichosis, with the effect largely lost 4 to 6 months after stopping [13]. A pooled safety analysis of six trials (680 bimatoprost users) reported mostly mild, local, reversible adverse events, including conjunctival redness, eyelid itching and eyelid pigmentation, with discontinuations of 3.2 percent versus 2.4 percent for vehicle [17]. A 20-person pilot of bimatoprost on eyebrows reported significant investigator-rated improvement versus vehicle [18].

Travoprost is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia, and generics are available in the UK [1]. Wikipedia lists it as a Novartis drug whose US labels are from Alcon [1]. Prostaglandin-based lash products sold as cosmetics are a separate regulatory category from the prescription eye drops.

In lash and brow-growth discussions, glaucoma prostaglandin drops are mentioned because their lash side effect is well known and because bimatoprost was approved for that purpose [3][5]. Travoprost is discussed as a member of that family, while the published cosmetic trials concern bimatoprost.

lore.intro: Discussion of travoprost in appearance contexts is a small branch of the wider conversation about prostaglandin lash growth, where the eyelash side effect of glaucoma drops is cited as the basis for lash and brow treatments [3][5].

claims.claim: Prostaglandin eye drops make eyelashes longer, thicker and darker.
Travoprost works on lashes the same way as bimatoprost or Latisse.
Lash gains stay once you have them.
The same drops can fill in sparse eyebrows or other hair.
Wiping off excess solution prevents unwanted darkening and growth around the eye.
Long-term use can change how the eye area looks, including a sunken or hollow upper lid.

timeline.event: Latanoprost, the first widely used prostaglandin F2-alpha eye drop, is approved in the US and EU [12].
Travoprost approved in the US and EU for lowering intraocular pressure [1].
Six randomized, double-masked trials of bimatoprost for eyelash hypotrichosis run in the US, Canada, UK and Japan [17].
A 278-person randomized trial reports bimatoprost 0.03% improving eyelash length, thickness and darkness versus vehicle [4].
Pilot trial of bimatoprost on eyebrows and patient-reported outcomes of lash treatment published [18][16].
A 12-month trial reports sustained lash effect during use and a fall-off 4 to 6 months after stopping [13].
A travoprost intracameral implant (iDose TR) is listed on DailyMed with a December 2023 label date [1].
Phase 3 results for the travoprost implant published [8]; a review proposes standardized staging of prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy [10].
